chief_complaint: sharp chest pain worsening when lying flat and relieved sitting forward
hpi_details: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with sharp chest pain worsening when lying flat and relieved sitting forward. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he has severe acid reflux or a strained chest muscle from sleeping in an awkward position on the couch.
concerns: He is worried that this sharp pain means he has a blockage that will require invasive open-heart surgery.
expectations: He hopes to receive strong anti-inflammatory painkillers so that he can finally lie down and sleep tonight.

investigation_events.title: ECG and inflammatory marker
investigation_events.availability_message: The ECG and C-reactive protein result are now available.

results.value: Diffuse concave ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression; no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Pericarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Plan for Acute Pericarditis: Obtain ECG (diffuse ST elevations), start high-dose Aspirin/Ibuprofen and Colchicine, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp chest pain worsening when lying flat and relieved sitting forward

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with sharp chest pain worsening when lying flat and relieved sitting forward. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Pericarditis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Pericarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness with neck vein distension — possible tamponade.
management_principles: Plan for Acute Pericarditis: Obtain ECG (diffuse ST elevations), start high-dose Aspirin/Ibuprofen and Colchicine
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Inflamed pericardium: sharp chest pain that hates lying flat and eases sitting forward, usually after a viral illness.
red_flags: Breathlessness with neck vein distension — possible tamponade

must_ask.say: Is it worse when you lie flat?
Does sitting up and leaning forward help?
Does breathing in deeply make it worse?
Have you been unwell with a virus recently?

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
When did it start, and how long does it last each time?

history.answer: My chest hurts with a sharp pain, and it gets a lot worse whenever I lie down flat.
It started gradually about two days ago while I was resting at home, and it has become steadily more painful.
The pain is right in the center of my chest, spread across the middle rather than one tiny point.
It is a sharp, stabbing ache, not a heavy squeezing or tearing sensation.
It radiates up toward my left shoulder and the side of my neck, but not down my arm or into my jaw.
The pain has been continuous for the past two days rather than coming and going in short spells.
It is around a six out of ten right now, but it spikes to an eight if I try to lie flat.
Resting does not make it go away, and walking slowly does not change it much, though changing body positions does.
It gets significantly worse when I take a deep breath, cough, or lie flat, and leaning forward gives me clear relief.
It is not related to eating or food, and I have no heartburn, acid regurgitation, or trouble swallowing.
I have not had cold sweats, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting spells.
I have felt slightly feverish and fatigued, but I do not have a persistent cough or any phlegm.
About a week ago, I had a bad cold with a runny nose, mild fever, and muscle aches that lasted a few days.
Neither leg is swollen or sore, and I have not had any recent surgeries, long trips, or periods of bed rest.
I have not noticed any rashes, blisters, or skin redness anywhere on my chest.
I feel anxious because of the chest pain, but I have not had sudden panic attacks or numbness in my hands.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and no one in my family had heart disease young.
I have never had chest pain like this in my life, and I have never had heart tests, catheterizations, or stents.
No, I have not hit my chest, and I have not done any heavy lifting, strenuous workouts, or repetitive strain.
Yes, I have been feeling unusually tired and run-down since this pain began.
I figured it was just really bad acid reflux or a pulled muscle from sleeping twisted on the couch.
I'm worried that there's a serious blockage in my chest and I'll end up needing open-heart surgery.
I'm hoping you can give me some strong pain relievers so I can actually lie flat and get some sleep tonight.
I have been completely healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter painkillers, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps a beer once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live in an apartment with my wife.
My parents are both alive and healthy, with no history of early heart disease or autoimmune disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg in right arm and 122/76 mmHg in left arm, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 37.6°C.
The patient appears fatigued and sits leaning slightly forward on the exam table for comfort, with no diaphoresis, cyanosis, or acute distress.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at 2 cm above the sternal angle with no jugular venous distension or Kussmaul sign.
No tenderness to palpation across the sternum, ribs, or costochondral junctions; pressure on the chest wall does not reproduce the pain.
A high-pitched, scratchy, three-component pericardial friction rub is heard best along the left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward; normal heart sounds with no murmurs.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields bilaterally.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, non-distended, with no epigastric tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly.
No peripheral edema in either lower extremity.
Both calves are soft, non-tender, with no swelling or erythema.
No skin rashes, vesicles, or localized lesions observed over the chest or back.
